pages.title: Workday To Acquire C1.ai To Expand Identity Governance For People And AI Agents
pages.text:
Workday To Acquire C1.ai To Expand Identity Governance For People And AI Agents
Workday has signed a definitive agreement to acquire C1.ai, an agentic identity platform that manages access to enterprise applications and systems for employees and AI agents.
The acquisition will expand Workday’s capabilities beyond managing workforce and agent records by adding identity-governance controls that determine what people and autonomous AI systems can access, when they receive access, and when permissions should be removed.
C1.ai connects with enterprise systems ranging from email and customer relationship management platforms to code repositories, financial applications, and cloud infrastructure. Its platform provisions scoped access, enforces organizational policies, incorporates human approvals, and maintains records of actions taken by people and agents.
Workday sees identity governance becoming increasingly important as businesses deploy more autonomous AI agents. The company cited C1.ai research indicating that 95% of large U.S. companies already use autonomous agents, while Deloitte research found that only 21% of organizations report having mature governance capabilities for those systems.
Workday plans to integrate C1.ai with its existing Agent System of Record. The combination would allow companies to move beyond simply registering and tracking AI agents by governing what those agents can access across Workday and other enterprise applications.
The technology could also automate access management throughout an employee’s lifecycle. When a new hire joins, they could receive permissions to applications such as Slack, Jira, and finance systems, while changes in job responsibilities could automatically trigger corresponding access updates. Permissions could then be removed when an employee leaves.
Similar controls would apply to AI agents. Agents acting on behalf of employees could receive more limited permissions than the person they support, while independently operating agents could be assigned broader but closely monitored access. Retired agents could have permissions revoked immediately rather than retaining access after their work ends.
Workday said the acquisition supports its broader strategy of becoming the identity governance layer for the combined human and AI workforce. The company currently serves more than 11,500 organizations worldwide, including more than 65% of the Fortune 500.
The transaction is expected to close in Workday’s fiscal fourth quarter of 2027, which ends January 31, 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.
Support: BofA Securities is serving as financial advisor to Workday, while Orrick is its legal advisor. Qatalyst is serving as financial advisor to C1.ai, and Ashurst Perkins Coie is serving as legal advisor.
KEY QUOTES:
“Today’s companies run on a combined workforce of people and AI agents. With C1.ai, we’ll help secure that workforce by managing and enforcing exactly who – and what – has access to connected apps and systems, giving each person and agent the right access at the right moment to make work easier, safer, and more compliant.”
Gerrit Kazmaier, President, Product And Technology Of Workday
“Enterprises can’t secure the AI era using yesterday’s IT tickets. Workday is the operational heart of the enterprise, and by bringing C1.ai’s identity governance directly into that core, we’ll be able to manage access for every human and agent in real time – making work faster without making it less secure.”

pages.title: Workday Channel Chief: Partners Are Key To AI And ‘Defining The Future Of Work’
pages.text:
Workday Channel Chief: Partners Are Key To AI And ‘Defining The Future Of Work’
In the wake of its Sana and C1.ai acquisitions, Workday is increasingly leveraging agentic AI to redefine HR and finance business processes. That’s changing the game—and creating opportunities—for the company’s channel partners, channel chief Bronwyn Hastings tells CRN.
Agentic AI is transforming financial and human resource management business processes and redefining how people work.
Workday, as a leading developer of enterprise finance, HR and payroll applications—and with a couple of agentic AI-related strategic acquisitions under its belt—is now a major player in providing the technology that’s driving that AI-fueled transformation.
And that means Workday’s channel partners, which today account for about 80 percent of Workday application implementations, are playing an increasingly important role in the success of those AI initiatives within many businesses and organizations.
[Related: Workday Launches AI Agent Deluge, Acquires Agentic Identity Startup]
“Partners have always been foundational for Workday,” said Bronwyn Hastings, who joined Workday in July as the company’s global channel chief, discussing the company’s agentic AI strategy in an interview with CRN. “What’s exciting is they’re becoming a core contributor to growth rather than an extension of growth.”
Partners are “being encouraged to lean into these new areas of being able to build agentic AI responses across HR and finance. It’s really allowing them to expand their businesses and [take] a more comprehensive approach to the future of work,” said Hastings (pictured), whose official title is senior vice president of global partners.
Hastings is a channel veteran who has held senior channel management posts at Docusign, UiPath, Google, Citrix, SAP and Oracle. In her interview with CRN, she noted that her resume includes experiences with application, software platform and agentic AI companies.
“Bringing all those three things together and then having the opportunity to define the future of work—who wouldn’t want to be a part of that?” she said.
KPMG, the global consulting and professional services company, is a longtime Workday strategic alliance partner that provides systems integration, cloud deployment and digital transformation services around Workday’s applications. (KPMG also just announced that it is adopting Workday internally as its own human resource management system.)
KPMG “really helps bridge the gap between what the platforms do and what our clients need,” and helps them leverage “the power of those insights and intelligence,” Chris Long, U.S. head of consulting and a principal at KPMG, told CRN. Much of that is provided through the KPMG Powered Delivery methodology, part of the company’s Powered Enterprise transformation framework.
“What we’re hearing from our clients, from an AI perspective, is that they’re really looking to move beyond isolated use cases and really lean into how they leverage the power of the data, the information, that is embedded in these Workday platforms” to meet business transformation goals, Long said.
Channel Impact Of AI Announcements At Workday Rising
This week at the Workday Rising conference in Las Vegas, the company launched a wave of new agentic AI products and platforms including autopilot agents that automate a range of functions across the company’s HR, payroll and financial management cloud applications.
Equally important was the news that Workday had struck a deal to buy C1.ai, a startup developer of leading-edge agentic identity technology for people and agents, in a move to boost the identity and access management capabilities of Workday’s applications.
The C1.ai acquisition deal, expected to be completed by Jan. 31, 2027, complements Workday’s $1.1 billion acquisition of Sana, developer of an AI-native enterprise knowledge management, workplace learning and conversational agent platform, in November 2025. At Rising this week Workday announced that Sana is the new agentic home screen and front-end user experience software for Workday applications.
No less important was Workday’s acquisition earlier this year of Pipedream and its integration platform that gives AI agents the ability to initiate workflows, pull data, and execute tasks across Workday and third-party applications.
The vision, Workday executives said at Rising, is that humans and AI agents will not just work side by side but collaborate within environments such as Workday. And partners will play a major role in making that a reality.
Workday’s AI initiatives provide a way for the company’s partner ecosystem to “become a driving contributor” to its AI strategy, not just a go-to-market extension, and bring value to customers, Hastings said. “It’s a very exciting time for partners to be leaning in with us.”
Workday works with a broad range of channel partners, more than 1,675 altogether, including global systems integrators, VARs and solution providers, MSPs, and ISVs, along with the major hyperscalers and leading data platform companies including Databricks and Snowflake. The company categorizes partners as advisory, innovation, services or MSP partners.
In addition to handling more than 80 percent of Workday implementation projects, partners today also source more than 30 percent of net-new annual contract value, Hastings said, up from a low single-figure percentage just a few years ago.
“It always takes the right partners with the right knowledge to really bring AI and agentic to life for customers with real use cases and real value,” Hastings said. The goal today is to ensure that “partners are deeply embedded with customers” to fully realize the benefits of AI.
KPMG is one of those partners. In addition to implementing Workday, KPMG helps businesses and organizations adopt industry best practices and, more recently, layering AI on top of that as clients look to make optimal use of enterprise data and their employees’ experience to improve decision making, Long said.
“And what’s important to our clients is making sure that they’re getting sustainable results and value from their investments,” he said.
Long said one of the biggest challenges around AI today is building client trust in the technology and its outputs. “CFOs and CROs are really looking to embed AI into everyone’s day-to-day work. And in order to connect it into that business process and help employees take action, you’ve got to have trust in the data,” he said.
PwC, the global professional services giant, also partners with Workday to provide business transformation services around the vendor’s HR and finance applications.
“But now with AI, it’s no longer just about transformation. It’s about agentic AI transformation and how you get there,” said Claudio Valera, global Workday practice leader at PwC, in an interview with CRN. “We’re seeing a lot of activity and a lot of interest and movement in the market right now around how to get value from their investment in Workday when it comes to agentic capabilities and just overall transformation capabilities.”
Expanding Initiatives With ‘Innovation’ Partners
Workday has been especially active over the last two years in expanding the number of “innovation” partners it works with, particularly systems integrators and ISV partners who integrate their products with Workday software (known as “build-with partners,” in Workday parlance) and those who develop products on the Workday platform (called “build-on” partners).
“Starting about two years ago, the way we think about developing, growing, curating the ISV ecosystem has taken on a lot more importance and significance for the growth of our business,” Mark Woollen, group vice president of partner innovation who heads up Workday’s ISV program, told CRN.
Build-on partners, now numbering about 170, develop Workday-native applications that extend the functionality of the vendor’s applications. They can orchestrate business processes for specific vertical industries, for example, or provide analytics capabilities that tap into Workday data for decision support tasks. Many ISVs make their products available through the Workday Marketplace and more than 60 have joined the Workday Agent Partner Network.
Woollen said PwC is one such innovation partner, leveraging its expertise in the healthcare space, for example, to develop a Workday-native physician compensation application.
The new agentic AI capabilities announced at Rising this week continue the evolution of Workday’s software into a “trusted agent platform” that ISVs can use to develop agentic applications.
“This is really important for our partners across the board, and in particular the ISV partners,” Woollen said. “It allows them to bring new innovation, new IP [intellectual property] to our shared clients and customers.”
He cited Auditoria, which develops finance automation software, and Censia, a developer of talent intelligence and workforce analytics apps, as examples of companies building agentic products on Workday. Customers, Woollen said, “need those agentic capabilities from the Auditorias and Censias of the world” while also seeking assurance that “they are trusted and that, effectively, as you’ve heard us say, they’re lawful agents.”
Woollen also stressed the importance to innovation partners of this week’s announcement that Workday is applying the Sana enterprise knowledge, learning and AI agent technology it acquired last year to be the new agentic home screen and front-end user experience software for the company’s cloud applications.
By providing a universal Workday user experience across both Workday and ISV applications, the new interface will make it easier for innovation partners to develop applications that tap into Workday workflows, Woollen said.
Channel chief Hastings noted that partners are very-well aware that agentic AI is disrupting “traditional deployment economics” and have responded by “moving away from routine configuration and maintenance” services and are expanding into higher-value “redesigning business” services such as developing agents for vertical industries, custom workflows, and specific personas such as CFOs.
Hastings acknowledged that all this requires some “agility of learning” for partners and Workday is providing assistance through “forward-deployed engineers” who work with partners as they develop agentic AI solutions and services.

pages.title: Workday faces growth threat as customers use Anthropic, Microsoft agents
pages.text:
Workday faces growth threat as customers use Anthropic, Microsoft agents
Third-party AI agents built on Claude and Copilot can tap Workday data directly, raising questions about who captures the value of enterprise automation
Workday spent years becoming the place where companies keep their most sensitive people and money data. Now some customers are reaching that data with AI agents Workday didn’t build.
Tools powered by Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft’s agent platforms can query Workday records directly, skipping Workday’s own AI products entirely.
Workday sells cloud software for human resources and finance. Its pitch for the AI era has centered on its own agents, which it has rebranded under the name Sana.
The problem is that external agents can do much of the same work. Agents running on Anthropic’s Claude, or built with Microsoft’s Copilot Studio and Azure AI Foundry, can read and act on Workday data without customers ever touching Workday’s AI tools.
The industry term for this risk is disintermediation. Put simply, a middle layer moves in between a vendor and its customers, and the vendor becomes plumbing.
So far, Workday’s own numbers don’t look like a company being sidelined. As of Q2 2026, over 5,500 customers were using Workday’s AI agents, a jump of more than 35% quarter-over-quarter.
Its AI SKUs also contribute close to $600 million in annual recurring revenue. That figure reflects growth of over 200% year-over-year.

Workday’s response: become the gatekeeper
Rather than trying to block outside agents, Workday has moved to govern them. Its main tool is the Agent System of Record, or ASOR.
ASOR works as a registry for AI agents, both Workday’s and everyone else’s. External agents get registered, tracked and overseen, with security controls, permission handling and audit trails built in.
Alongside ASOR sits the Agent Gateway, which handles connections from outside agents. Workday supports interoperability standards including Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A).
Workday also lets customers decide how external agents get in. Access can be configured as delegate or ambient, depending on permissions. Delegate access generally means an agent acts on behalf of a specific person. Ambient access is broader, letting an agent operate in the background within its granted permissions.
Microsoft is part of this arrangement rather than purely a threat. Under a partnership between the two companies, agents built on Microsoft’s platforms can register in ASOR for unified tracking and governance.
CEO Aneel Bhusri has acknowledged the financial potential in monetizing agent access. Workday has built an Agent Management Hub and APIs designed for configuring external agents, signaling it sees outside agents as a revenue line, not just a security headache.
For investors, the story splits into two tracks. The near-term track looks healthy: a customer count past 5,500, quarterly growth above 35% and AI revenue approaching $600 million.
Workday’s counter is a platform play. If you can’t guarantee customers use your agents, make sure every agent runs through your registry, your gateway and your permission system.
What to watch next: how Workday prices external agent access, how many third-party agents get registered in ASOR, and whether growth in Sana adoption holds its pace as Anthropic and Microsoft tools spread.

Metaview, the Agentic Recruiting Platform trusted by more than 7,000 companies, today announced an expanded two-way integration with Workday, the enterprise AI platform for HR, finance and IT. The announcement builds on Metaview's growing traction among enterprise and Fortune 500 companies, enabling organizations to deploy AI agents across recruiting while maintaining their existing systems, security, and controls.
Workday serves more than 11,500 global customers, including over 65% of the Fortune 500. The expanded integration brings Metaview's AI agents directly into Workday Recruiting, extending beyond sourcing to application review, interviewing, and feedback.

Building on Metaview's existing Workday Sourcing integration, recruiting teams can now:
Review applications at scale: Metaview's Application Review Agent assesses inbound applicants and syncs advancement and rejection decisions directly into Workday.
Capture interviews and automate feedback: Metaview generates recruiting-specific notes and automatically fills Workday scorecards using existing interview templates. Interviewers can access notes, recordings, and transcripts through Metaview's browser extension without leaving Workday.
Preserve existing workflows: Approvals, candidate dispositions, and audit trails continue to run when Metaview advances or rejects a candidate.
Enterprise-grade AI orchestration with human oversight
As large organizations move from experimenting with AI to deploying agents across critical business functions, security, governance, and control are essential.
Metaview's platform is designed to meet enterprise requirements, enabling organizations to:
Set clear guardrails defining what agents can and cannot do using company knowledge, policies, and rules.
Maintain human oversight over critical recruiting decisions.
Automatically flag inconsistencies or non-compliant behavior.
Access full audit trails of agent reasoning, actions, and outputs.
Protect candidate data with SOC 2 Type II compliance, SSO, and enterprise privacy controls.
"As Metaview increasingly serves enterprise and Fortune 500 companies, we're focused on making AI agents work within the systems and security requirements these organizations already trust," said Siadhal Magos, co-founder and CEO of Metaview. We're combining powerful AI orchestration with human oversight, so teams can automate more of the recruiting admin without compromising control."
For enterprises managing thousands of applicants and complex hiring processes, AI agents offer an opportunity to reduce operational work without introducing disconnected tools or sacrificing human judgment.

pages.title: Workday’s Gerrit Kazmaier on why AI won’t take the human out of work
pages.text:
Home » Feature Story » General » Workday’s Gerrit Kazmaier on why AI won’t take the human out of work
Workday’s Gerrit Kazmaier on why AI won’t take the human out of work
Workday's Gerrit Kazmaier calls AI at work "the great liberation"
Workday draws firm lines on where humans stay in control
JLL's transformation chief says changing human behaviour is the real hurdle
Every few years, hasn’t a new tech innovation promised to give us our time back? And still we end up being busier than before! Email was supposed to reduce official memos, collaboration tools were supposed to kill email, and now AI agents are entering the conversation. Especially in HR tech.
✅ Thank you for completing the survey!
Besides all the productivity and efficiency wins, when software starts screening resumes, scheduling interviews and clearing expense reports by itself, an inevitable question arises. If AI takes over so much of the work, what’s left of the human side of it? Is AI the end of serendipity at work?
I put that question to Gerrit Kazmaier, President, Product and Technology at Workday, during a select media roundtable. He didn’t hesitate in his response, “I actually think it’s the great liberation. And I think it’s actually what brings back fun and excitement and engagement at work. The reality today is most time at work is spent on work about work: over-alignment, over-coordination, waiting for approvals, handovers. A recruiter not thinking about and engaging with talent, but reading through resumes or scheduling interviews. Or a financial analyst spending the day downloading data and finding the right data, versus really developing new ideas on how they could grow the business.”
According to Kazmaier, the risk isn’t that AI will strip work of its humanity. Because modern work has already lost a good deal of it – bogged down under status updates, coordination calls and waiting for approvals. Customer success teams, Kazmaier pointed out, are a case in point.
“When you look into what customer success managers are doing, they’re not really engaging with customers. They’re not really being strategic advisors. They are not really working on the next big project with them. They’re actually stuck reading emails, documents, PowerPoints, getting status, aligning status,” he said.
True growth with AI, not just operational efficiency
This is where Workday wants to differentiate itself from others. Plenty of enterprises see AI as a cost-cutting exercise, which is thinking way too small, argues Kazmaier.
“There is a world where some companies think about AI as a pure efficiency game. Look at all the things that you do and just make them faster and cheaper. Workday is very different, we think of AI as a growth opportunity,” said Kazmaier. “We think about AI in a way that allows you to unlock new market opportunities, have insanely good customer retention, do more and do it faster, because we are giving you back so much time through the AI automation we can drive in that mundane category of work.”
Also read: Workday CEO Aneel Bhusri calls Oracle, SAP as AI ‘dinosaurs’
To drive his point home, Kazmaier highlighted the industry’s fascination with fully self-running companies. “Frankly, some companies dream of an autonomous enterprise. We think that’s a very cold and soulless way to think about an enterprise,” he said.
Cold and soulless are, of course, strong words. Especially from someone whose job is to build AI that runs hiring, payroll and finance for some of the world’s largest companies. However, for Kazmaier, it all boils down to one thing – that people, not algorithms, are the real multiplier. “We think that talent, the people, that’s your ultimate growth driver with AI. And we know from research that great talent drives amazing outcomes with AI.”
Where ‘almost right’ is wrong in AI-enabled workflows
Of course, liberation from the drudgery of work only works if you can trust the machine doing the liberating. And in HR and finance, the margin for error is razor thin, and the stakes are always high, something that Kazmaier perfectly understands.
“We know we are in a space where almost right is wrong. And I think this is actually one of the biggest challenges our customers have when they’re trying to apply AI, because they’re applying it to mission-critical processes, like paying people, like making hiring decisions,” emphasised Kazmaier.
Workday’s answer is a three-tier framework – human in the loop, human on the loop, and human out of the loop – mapped to how much a given decision affects a person’s life.
“There are jobs where we want humans to have ultimate oversight, like a hiring decision – everything which materially influences the income or employment of a person. There are humans on the loop, which means they are informed about actions that AI systems take. A classical example would be travel and expense management approvals. And then there are systems where the human should be out of the loop. For instance, transaction sampling and financial compliance of accounting records. And the reason is that AI is accurate enough, way more accurate than a human ever could be. It’s doing it in real time. No person can do it. And it’s not directly impacting a human or a person’s access to opportunity.”
Hiring sits firmly in the first bucket. Interview scheduling doesn’t – and the reasoning behind that is surprisingly human, according to Kazmaier.
“Workday does not automate hiring decisions, because we ultimately think it’s always going to be a human-in-the-loop decision. There is more to this than just algorithmic judgment. But what we decide to do automatically is interview coordination and scheduling. And there is a simple reason for that. People apply for their next job when they are usually done working in their current job. That’s the time most recruiters don’t work, because they finish their workday too. So sometimes they have to wait a day or even a weekend.”
In other words, taking the human out of the loop here isn’t about replacing the recruiter. It’s about not losing a great candidate because everyone on the hiring side happened to be offline on a Saturday.
That’s precisely the problem JLL set out to fix. The global real estate services firm, and a Workday customer since 2018, JLL rolled out its recruitment agent (called HireBuddy) globally just this summer. Jane Curran, Chief Transformation Officer, JLL, explained why hiring was the obvious place to start.
“We’re 111,000 and we hire about 30,000 people a year… This summer was the time when we launched the whole thing globally end-to-end, not just automated interview scheduling, which is amazing, but also rethinking how you hire for high-volume positions, and how you redo the recruiter’s experience and the manager’s experience, and ultimately the candidate’s, because some of these people are on the market for 10 days. So you don’t want to lose out because you have a bad, slow process,” highlighted Curran.
Ultimately the process drives results, AI only assists
Underpinning all of this is what Kazmaier calls “lawful AI” – a design philosophy where AI doesn’t run the show on its own. It’s dictated by the process governing the principles at play.
“When we apply AI, we design it in a way that we don’t have an AI system driving a process. We have a deterministic process that is using AI at points where we can use AI judgment instead of waiting for a human operator. That’s a very different way to look at AI automation. Because repeatability, auditability, traceability are all things that we want to have guaranteed. That’s what we mean when we say lawful AI,” according to Kazmaier.
It’s a subtle but important distinction, and it makes sense, if you think about it. AI as a component inside a governed workflow, rather than the workflow itself. And on the customer side, those guardrails need their own checks. Lavanya VNV, Director, Product Management, JLL, described how her team keeps tabs on what the AI is doing – and why. “We made sure that AI has guardrails. We are also capturing its reasoning on why it is telling what it is telling. And we have audit processes, which go and check the intent of the AI… We’re also realising that delegating work to AI also means there’s a lot of work in checking AI’s work,” emphasized Lavanya.
If the guardrails settle who decides, the bigger question is how work itself should change. This is where Kazmaier offered his most interesting idea and a sharp diagnosis of why so many AI rollouts underwhelm.
Also read: Workday opens its platform to AI agents: Autopilot Agents and Headless Access explained
“The interesting thing with even the frontier AI models is that they are hyper-proficient in some of those aspects, and in some aspects they are not. This is what’s called the jagged line of AI. It’s really hard to predict sometimes. So when a customer of ours comes to us and says, ‘How do I apply AI to my work?’, we have to understand work differently. We have to understand work through the lens of AI automation. And that’s not skills. That’s not workflows. That is the fundamental task,” explained Kazmaier
Break a job down to that level, according to Kazmaier, and every task falls into one of three buckets. “Once you disaggregate your work into tasks, you basically see three pools. One pool is AI can automate this task. A second pool is that AI can assist the task. And the third pool is that it is a task that humans do best, or that you want humans to do,” he said.
That’s the job of Workday’s Work Intelligence, which maps a company’s existing job profiles into tasks and projects which ones AI can automate, assist with, or leave to people. Once you do that, something unexpected happens to the job titles themselves.
“What we see right now is that the job profiles rearrange. Product manager, software engineer, designer – they’re more or less becoming the same, because we took the coding part and using a design tool out of all of these specialised profiles. Now you have a converged profile which is much more flexible.”
At JLL, Curran sees the same shift playing out inside HR itself, where thousands of people currently spend their days answering routine queries.
“In the age of AI, orgs are changing, skills are changing. In HR, we would like those people to be focusing on: how do I reskill the people I have? How do I design new organisations? That’s where we want humans working in HR, and not on highly repeatable tasks.”
Which brings us back to serendipity. And whether an algorithm can spot the candidate whose resume doesn’t tick every box, but who might be exactly the right hire? Kazmaier turned the question on its head.
“We should not underestimate the efficacy of a well-designed AI system. The question really is the other way around. How do you specify what your company culture is, what that thing is that makes you as a company uniquely you, what you’re looking for, in a way that an agentic solution can support? Because that’s possible. Why does great talent become the biggest leverage for AI? Because they can actually paint that picture.”
Still, not everyone on the front lines finds an AI-saturated workday purely liberating, as evidenced by Lavanya’s refreshingly honest take on what it feels like to spend your days surrounded by agents. “Personally, as a techie, when I have a personal agent, Claude Code and so many other things with me, it can sometimes actually be daunting not to work with people who speak to you, and you’re already working with agents,” she revealed.
And for Curran, the biggest risk in JLL’s AI journey isn’t the technology at all. “The tech will work. We can clean the data. We can rewrite the process. But I’ve got to change hearts and minds to say this is better than that,” said Curran.
It’s a telling reminder that the “great liberation” Kazmaier describes won’t arrive just because the agents are ready. Workday’s vision for the next generation of ERP depends on people choosing to work differently too. If Workda

pages.title: Workday goes headless; CIOs must lay the groundwork
pages.text:
Workday goes headless; CIOs must lay the groundwork
The vendor unveiled an agentic AI and headless push, highlighting why high-fidelity data and CIO leadership are essential for success.
Myles Suer,CIO Analyst and Tech Journalist
Workday CEO and co-founder Aneel Bhusri speaks at Workday Rising 2026.Photo courtesy Workday
LAS VEGAS — Coming into Workday Rising, I wondered about the company's prospects. Recent quarterly results showed a near 13% increase in revenue. At the same time, Workday has been cutting head count.
At its annual user conference this week, Workday CEO and co-founder Aneel Bhusri insisted the cuts were made to improve business agility and reporting.
"We had 13 levels between me and a developer, and we offer middle managers individual contributor roles," he said during a press Q&A after the keynote. Bhusri returned to the helm in February.
At the same time, speculation that Workday has been in discussions about taking the company private continues to swirl. If Workday goes private, this will, without question, be an outgrowth of the SaaSpocalypse, where generative AI created market panic for SaaS business models. But what will the company gain?
Workday has dominated the enterprise human capital management (HCM) market and, to a lesser degree, cloud-based ERP. My question coming into Workday Rising was: Can the vendor pivot to the AI shift?
Related:Even now, ERP implementations can make or break CIOs
My answer, in a word, is yes.
Despite Hurricane Isaias disrupting travel in Las Vegas, the conference brought together 17,000 HR, ERP and IT professionals who likely wanted to hear about the disruptive changes coming to HR and the business functions HR supports.
It was clear from my conversations: Workday is fully engaging the technology trends of the time to address those disruptions — by not only automating AI agents but also introducing headless capabilities.
This embrace of headless was refreshing to see, given this is where applications supported by agentic AI are likely headed, and some vendors are slower to move in that direction. Last week, for example, SAP's president of products discussed with me how it's only exposing APIs as a move to headless. In Workday's case, the company is not only going headless, but it is also surrounding its architecture with an agent platform and developer resources to support anyone building on its code base interface agents.
It's an aggressive step for Workday that recognizes the benefit of separating back-end tech stack from the front-end capabilities. Unlike Salesforce, which highlighted at Dreamforce its push toward headless and toward becoming the UI of choice, Workday is not ready to announce that it is disinvesting from the GUI. Workday, on the other hand, expanded Sana across the enterprise. The agentic experience and orchestration platform is based on technology the company acquired in 2025; it uses the Model Context Protocol to operate within third-party AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot, Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise and Slack.
Related:Dreamforce opens with AI, but questions for CIOs remain
Workday is providing knowledge workers immediate agentic experiences to complete work, not just answer questions. Employees can make requests in natural language and have agents act on them directly. A concierge agent, for example, can resolve HR and IT requests, such as onboarding and password resets, before they become help desk tickets. This could provide tangible labor cost savings.
Workday's announcements also included automating AI agents to work continuously in the background across IT, finance, compliance and HR. The company also introduced a talent acquisition autopilot agent, which is now in early access. Workday said these agents are coded with a company's policies, permissions and approval rules so they can advise or act within each workers' policies and approval limits. Workday said its goal is to free up teams to focus on decisions that require human judgment.
Time will tell.
Workday also announced it is acquiring C1.ai, an agentic identity platform for people and agents, following another trend. As the software industry becomes dependent on AI foundation models, application and data vendors are buying the access and security layer. For Workday, the acquisition makes sense: HR is where roles and privileges are defined. But it also suggests application vendors aren't waiting for security vendors to catch up and create the appropriate guardrails.
Related:How AI agents broke traditional SaaS pricing
Given the product news and in my conversations with attendees, one theme stood out to me: This is a moment that calls for CIO skills.
Bhusri put it plainly during a press Q&A: "None of this works without high-quality data."
This is critical to creating the context. Just as humans need it to do their jobs well, AI needs high-fidelity data, a semantic layer and an ontology. CIOs are crucial to building that foundational data layer and helping HR define the business context that gives the data meaning. For Workday, its Zero-Copy Data In layer, which enables users to query external data where it resides, is built on data corrected and mastered in systems such as Snowflake that CIOs and their teams manage. And this matters because with finance and accounting, there is zero margin for error.
Beyond building the foundation for the data cloud, CIOs and their teams are needed to ensure the supporting APIs are in place to pull other data sources, along with governance for APIs, data and processes. They are also essential to solving larger transformation challenges that extend beyond HR.
Part of that work is keeping the corporate data harness secure and operational, which means confirming guardrails work as planned and are validated regularly.
From the #CIOChat that I hosted for years, vanguard IT leaders have always worked closely with their chief human resources officers. This was especially the case as the COVID-19 pandemic hit and companies needed to operate on digital platforms.
But this hasn't been a universal experience. During #CIOChat, I observed two types of CIOs: The first had a strong relationship with business leaders and worked to solve business problems; the second focused on technology and have since been pushed out of the role.
"When human capital management solutions were managed on-premises, IT played a significant role in managing those systems," Dave Eberhardt, partner for HR transformation at PwC, told me. This was at a time when some CIOs focused solely on infrastructure. As HCM systems pivoted to the cloud, technology ownership shifted from IT to HR, he added.
I asked Isaac Sacolick, former McGraw Hill Construction CIO, about this. Sacolick said, "At that time, too many CIOs, unfortunately, were infrastructure-related. But it was not all of them."
It's time to close that gap.
David Wachtel, general manager of core HR products at Workday, said CIOs can play a meaningful role. He said CHROs "would be … welcoming of CIOs who wanted to help. CHROs would breathe a welcome sigh of relief. They honestly would appreciate the outreach and desire to play together."
It is time for CIOs to dig in and understand the HR piece of the tech stack as it increasingly is about agents and relating them and human workers together. CIOs who are just about infrastructure are no longer valuable to their companies.
Workday Rising provided a look at the company's push to make its platforms and capabilities headless. Is your company looking for that kind of flexibility in its technology stack? Let us know at [email protected].
Myles Suer is a CIO analyst and tech journalist. Recognized by Leadtail as a top CIO influencer, he is the former leader of #CIOChat, a global community connecting CIOs and senior technology leaders. His insights have been featured in publications such as CMSWire, CIO.com, VKTR, and Cutter Business Technology Journal. Suer frequently reviews books on AI, technology, and business strategy from leading publishers, including Harvard Business Review Press, MIT Press, and Columbia University Press. Metaview, the Agentic Recruiting Platform trusted by more than 7,000 companies, today announced an expanded two-way integration with Workday, the enterprise AI platform for HR, finance and IT. Bringing agentic recruiting into enterprise workflows
Building on Metaview's existing Workday Sourcing integration, recruiting teams can now:
Review applications at scale: Metaview's Application Review Agent assesses inbound applicants and syncs advancement and rejection decisions directly into Workday.
Capture interviews and automate feedback: Metaview generates recruiting-specific notes and automatically fills Workday scorecards using existing interview templates. Interviewers can access notes, recordings, and transcripts through Metaview's browser extension without leaving Workday.
Preserve existing workflows: Approvals, candidate dispositions, and audit trails continue to run when Metaview advances or rejects a candidate.
Enterprise-grade AI orchestration with human oversight

Metaview's platform is designed to meet enterprise requirements, enabling organizations to:
Set clear guardrails defining what agents can and cannot do using company knowledge, policies, and rules.
Maintain human oversight over critical recruiting decisions.
Automatically flag inconsistencies or non-compliant behavior.
Access full audit trails of agent reasoning, actions, and outputs.
Protect candidate data with SOC 2 Type II compliance, SSO, and enterprise privacy controls.
"As Metaview increasingly serves enterprise and Fortune 500 companies, we're focused on making AI agents work within the systems and security requirements these organizations already trust," said Siadhal Magos, co-founder and CEO of Metaview. "With Workday serving more than 65% of the Fortune 500, this integration is an important step in bringing agentic recruiting to the world's largest organizations. We're combining powerful AI orchestration with human oversight, so teams can automate more of the recruiting admin without compromising control."

Workday’s Gerrit Kazmaier on why AI won’t take the human out of work
Workday's Gerrit Kazmaier calls AI at work "the great liberation"
Workday draws firm lines on where humans stay in control
JLL's transformation chief says changing human behaviour is the real hurdle
Every few years, hasn’t a new tech innovation promised to give us our time back? And still we end up being busier than before! Email was supposed to reduce official memos, collaboration tools were supposed to kill email, and now AI agents are entering the conversation. Especially in HR tech.

Besides all the productivity and efficiency wins, when software starts screening resumes, scheduling interviews and clearing expense reports by itself, an inevitable question arises. If AI takes over so much of the work, what’s left of the human side of it? Is AI the end of serendipity at work?
I put that question to Gerrit Kazmaier, President, Product and Technology at Workday, during a select media roundtable. He didn’t hesitate in his response, “I actually think it’s the great liberation. And I think it’s actually what brings back fun and excitement and engagement at work. The reality today is most time at work is spent on work about work: over-alignment, over-coordination, waiting for approvals, handovers. A recruiter not thinking about and engaging with talent, but reading through resumes or scheduling interviews. Or a financial analyst spending the day downloading data and finding the right data, versus really developing new ideas on how they could grow the business.”
According to Kazmaier, the risk isn’t that AI will strip work of its humanity. Because modern work has already lost a good deal of it – bogged down under status updates, coordination calls and waiting for approvals. Customer success teams, Kazmaier pointed out, are a case in point.
“When you look into what customer success managers are doing, they’re not really engaging with customers. They’re not really being strategic advisors. They are not really working on the next big project with them. They’re actually stuck reading emails, documents, PowerPoints, getting status, aligning status,” he said.
True growth with AI, not just operational efficiency
This is where Workday wants to differentiate itself from others. Plenty of enterprises see AI as a cost-cutting exercise, which is thinking way too small, argues Kazmaier.
“There is a world where some companies think about AI as a pure efficiency game. Look at all the things that you do and just make them faster and cheaper. Workday is very different, we think of AI as a growth opportunity,” said Kazmaier. “We think about AI in a way that allows you to unlock new market opportunities, have insanely good customer retention, do more and do it faster, because we are giving you back so much time through the AI automation we can drive in that mundane category of work.”

To drive his point home, Kazmaier highlighted the industry’s fascination with fully self-running companies. “Frankly, some companies dream of an autonomous enterprise. We think that’s a very cold and soulless way to think about an enterprise,” he said.
Cold and soulless are, of course, strong words. Especially from someone whose job is to build AI that runs hiring, payroll and finance for some of the world’s largest companies. However, for Kazmaier, it all boils down to one thing – that people, not algorithms, are the real multiplier. “We think that talent, the people, that’s your ultimate growth driver with AI. And we know from research that great talent drives amazing outcomes with AI.”
Where ‘almost right’ is wrong in AI-enabled workflows
Of course, liberation from the drudgery of work only works if you can trust the machine doing the liberating. And in HR and finance, the margin for error is razor thin, and the stakes are always high, something that Kazmaier perfectly understands.
“We know we are in a space where almost right is wrong. And I think this is actually one of the biggest challenges our customers have when they’re trying to apply AI, because they’re applying it to mission-critical processes, like paying people, like making hiring decisions,” emphasised Kazmaier.
Workday’s answer is a three-tier framework – human in the loop, human on the loop, and human out of the loop – mapped to how much a given decision affects a person’s life.
“There are jobs where we want humans to have ultimate oversight, like a hiring decision – everything which materially influences the income or employment of a person. There are humans on the loop, which means they are informed about actions that AI systems take. A classical example would be travel and expense management approvals. And then there are systems where the human should be out of the loop. For instance, transaction sampling and financial compliance of accounting records. And the reason is that AI is accurate enough, way more accurate than a human ever could be. It’s doing it in real time. No person can do it. And it’s not directly impacting a human or a person’s access to opportunity.”
Hiring sits firmly in the first bucket. Interview scheduling doesn’t – and the reasoning behind that is surprisingly human, according to Kazmaier.
“Workday does not automate hiring decisions, because we ultimately think it’s always going to be a human-in-the-loop decision. There is more to this than just algorithmic judgment. But what we decide to do automatically is interview coordination and scheduling. And there is a simple reason for that. People apply for their next job when they are usually done working in their current job. That’s the time most recruiters don’t work, because they finish their workday too. So sometimes they have to wait a day or even a weekend.”
In other words, taking the human out of the loop here isn’t about replacing the recruiter. It’s about not losing a great candidate because everyone on the hiring side happened to be offline on a Saturday.
That’s precisely the problem JLL set out to fix. The global real estate services firm, and a Workday customer since 2018, JLL rolled out its recruitment agent (called HireBuddy) globally just this summer. Jane Curran, Chief Transformation Officer, JLL, explained why hiring was the obvious place to start.
“We’re 111,000 and we hire about 30,000 people a year… This summer was the time when we launched the whole thing globally end-to-end, not just automated interview scheduling, which is amazing, but also rethinking how you hire for high-volume positions, and how you redo the recruiter’s experience and the manager’s experience, and ultimately the candidate’s, because some of these people are on the market for 10 days. So you don’t want to lose out because you have a bad, slow process,” highlighted Curran.
Ultimately the process drives results, AI only assists
Underpinning all of this is what Kazmaier calls “lawful AI” – a design philosophy where AI doesn’t run the show on its own. It’s dictated by the process governing the principles at play.
“When we apply AI, we design it in a way that we don’t have an AI system driving a process. We have a deterministic process that is using AI at points where we can use AI judgment instead of waiting for a human operator. That’s a very different way to look at AI automation. Because repeatability, auditability, traceability are all things that we want to have guaranteed. That’s what we mean when we say lawful AI,” according to Kazmaier.
It’s a subtle but important distinction, and it makes sense, if you think about it. AI as a component inside a governed workflow, rather than the workflow itself. And on the customer side, those guardrails need their own checks. Lavanya VNV, Director, Product Management, JLL, described how her team keeps tabs on what the AI is doing – and why. “We made sure that AI has guardrails. We are also capturing its reasoning on why it is telling what it is telling. And we have audit processes, which go and check the intent of the AI… We’re also realising that delegating work to AI also means there’s a lot of work in checking AI’s work,” emphasized Lavanya.
If the guardrails settle who decides, the bigger question is how work itself should change. This is where Kazmaier offered his most interesting idea and a sharp diagnosis of why so many AI rollouts underwhelm.

“The interesting thing with even the frontier AI models is that they are hyper-proficient in some of those aspects, and in some aspects they are not. This is what’s called the jagged line of AI. It’s really hard to predict sometimes. So when a customer of ours comes to us and says, ‘How do I apply AI to my work?’, we have to understand work differently. We have to understand work through the lens of AI automation. And that’s not skills. That’s not workflows. That is the fundamental task,” explained Kazmaier
Break a job down to that level, according to Kazmaier, and every task falls into one of three buckets. “Once you disaggregate your work into tasks, you basically see three pools. One pool is AI can automate this task. A second pool is that AI can assist the task. And the third pool is that it is a task that humans do best, or that you want humans to do,” he said.
That’s the job of Workday’s Work Intelligence, which maps a company’s existing job profiles into tasks and projects which ones AI can automate, assist with, or leave to people. Once you do that, something unexpected happens to the job titles themselves.
“What we see right now is that the job profiles rearrange. Product manager, software engineer, designer – they’re more or less becoming the same, because we took the coding part and using a design tool out of all of these specialised profiles. Now you have a converged profile which is much more flexible.”
At JLL, Curran sees the same shift playing out inside HR itself, where thousands of people currently spend their days answering routine queries.
“In the age of AI, orgs are changing, skills are changing. In HR, we would like those people to be focusing on: how do I reskill the people I have? How do I design new organisations? That’s where we want humans working in HR, and not on highly repeatable tasks.”
Which brings us back to serendipity. And whether an algorithm can spot the candidate whose resume doesn’t tick every box, but who might be exactly the right hire? Kazmaier turned the question on its head.
“We should not underestimate the efficacy of a well-designed AI system. The question really is the other way around. How do you specify what your company culture is, what that thing is that makes you as a company uniquely you, what you’re looking for, in a way that an agentic solution can support? Because that’s possible. Why does great talent become the biggest leverage for AI? Because they can actually paint that picture.”
Still, not everyone on the front lines finds an AI-saturated workday purely liberating, as evidenced by Lavanya’s refreshingly honest take on what it feels like to spend your days surrounded by agents. “Personally, as a techie, when I have a personal agent, Claude Code and so many other things with me, it can sometimes actually be daunting not to work with people who speak to you, and you’re already working with agents,” she revealed.
And for Curran, the biggest risk in JLL’s AI journey isn’t the technology at all. “The tech will work. We can clean the data. We can rewrite the process. But I’ve got to change hearts and minds to say this is better than that,” said Curran.
It’s a telling reminder that the “great liberation” Kazmaier describes won’t arrive just because the agents are ready. Workday’s vision for the next generation of ERP depends on people choosing to work differently too. The vendor unveiled an agentic AI and headless push, highlighting why high-fidelity data and CIO leadership are essential for success.
Myles Suer,CIO Analyst and Tech Journalist
Workday CEO and co-founder Aneel Bhusri speaks at Workday Rising 2026.Photo courtesy Workday
LAS VEGAS — Coming into Workday Rising, I wondered about the company's prospects. Recent quarterly results showed a near 13% increase in revenue. At the same time, Workday has been cutting head count.
At its annual user conference this week, Workday CEO and co-founder Aneel Bhusri insisted the cuts were made to improve business agility and reporting.
"We had 13 levels between me and a developer, and we offer middle managers individual contributor roles," he said during a press Q&A after the keynote. Bhusri returned to the helm in February.
At the same time, speculation that Workday has been in discussions about taking the company private continues to swirl. If Workday goes private, this will, without question, be an outgrowth of the SaaSpocalypse, where generative AI created market panic for SaaS business models. But what will the company gain?
Workday has dominated the enterprise human capital management (HCM) market and, to a lesser degree, cloud-based ERP. My question coming into Workday Rising was: Can the vendor pivot to the AI shift?
Related:Even now, ERP implementations can make or break CIOs
My answer, in a word, is yes.
Despite Hurricane Isaias disrupting travel in Las Vegas, the conference brought together 17,000 HR, ERP and IT professionals who likely wanted to hear about the disruptive changes coming to HR and the business functions HR supports.
It was clear from my conversations: Workday is fully engaging the technology trends of the time to address those disruptions — by not only automating AI agents but also introducing headless capabilities.
This embrace of headless was refreshing to see, given this is where applications supported by agentic AI are likely headed, and some vendors are slower to move in that direction. Last week, for example, SAP's president of products discussed with me how it's only exposing APIs as a move to headless. In Workday's case, the company is not only going headless, but it is also surrounding its architecture with an agent platform and developer resources to support anyone building on its code base interface agents.
It's an aggressive step for Workday that recognizes the benefit of separating back-end tech stack from the front-end capabilities. Unlike Salesforce, which highlighted at Dreamforce its push toward headless and toward becoming the UI of choice, Workday is not ready to announce that it is disinvesting from the GUI. Workday, on the other hand, expanded Sana across the enterprise. The agentic experience and orchestration platform is based on technology the company acquired in 2025; it uses the Model Context Protocol to operate within third-party AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot, Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise and Slack.
Related:Dreamforce opens with AI, but questions for CIOs remain
Workday is providing knowledge workers immediate agentic experiences to complete work, not just answer questions. Employees can make requests in natural language and have agents act on them directly. A concierge agent, for example, can resolve HR and IT requests, such as onboarding and password resets, before they become help desk tickets. This could provide tangible labor cost savings.
Workday's announcements also included automating AI agents to work continuously in the background across IT, finance, compliance and HR. The company also introduced a talent acquisition autopilot agent, which is now in early access. Workday said these agents are coded with a company's policies, permissions and approval rules so they can advise or act within each workers' policies and approval limits. Workday said its goal is to free up teams to focus on decisions that require human judgment.
Time will tell.
Workday also announced it is acquiring C1.ai, an agentic identity platform for people and agents, following another trend. As the software industry becomes dependent on AI foundation models, application and data vendors are buying the access and security layer. For Workday, the acquisition makes sense: HR is where roles and privileges are defined. But it also suggests application vendors aren't waiting for security vendors to catch up and create the appropriate guardrails.
Related:How AI agents broke traditional SaaS pricing
Given the product news and in my conversations with attendees, one theme stood out to me: This is a moment that calls for CIO skills.
Bhusri put it plainly during a press Q&A: "None of this works without high-quality data."
This is critical to creating the context. Just as humans need it to do their jobs well, AI needs high-fidelity data, a semantic layer and an ontology. CIOs are crucial to building that foundational data layer and helping HR define the business context that gives the data meaning. For Workday, its Zero-Copy Data In layer, which enables users to query external data where it resides, is built on data corrected and mastered in systems such as Snowflake that CIOs and their teams manage. And this matters because with finance and accounting, there is zero margin for error.
Beyond building the foundation for the data cloud, CIOs and their teams are needed to ensure the supporting APIs are in place to pull other data sources, along with governance for APIs, data and processes. They are also essential to solving larger transformation challenges that extend beyond HR.
Part of that work is keeping the corporate data harness secure and operational, which means confirming guardrails work as planned and are validated regularly.
From the #CIOChat that I hosted for years, vanguard IT leaders have always worked closely with their chief human resources officers. This was especially the case as the COVID-19 pandemic hit and companies needed to operate on digital platforms.
But this hasn't been a universal experience. During #CIOChat, I observed two types of CIOs: The first had a strong relationship with business leaders and worked to solve business problems; the second focused on technology and have since been pushed out of the role.
"When human capital management solutions were managed on-premises, IT played a significant role in managing those systems," Dave Eberhardt, partner for HR transformation at PwC, told me. This was at a time when some CIOs focused solely on infrastructure. As HCM systems pivoted to the cloud, technology ownership shifted from IT to HR, he added.
I asked Isaac Sacolick, former McGraw Hill Construction CIO, about this. Sacolick said, "At that time, too many CIOs, unfortunately, were infrastructure-related. But it was not all of them."
It's time to close that gap.
David Wachtel, general manager of core HR products at Workday, said CIOs can play a meaningful role. He said CHROs "would be … welcoming of CIOs who wanted to help. CHROs would breathe a welcome sigh of relief. They honestly would appreciate the outreach and desire to play together."
It is time for CIOs to dig in and understand the HR piece of the tech stack as it increasingly is about agents and relating them and human workers together. CIOs who are just about infrastructure are no longer valuable to their companies.

bear_case: Workday faces significant risks including integration challenges with C1.ai, potential legal challenges regarding algorithmic bias in its hiring tools, and concerns that HR tech budgets may lag broader AI adoption, delaying revenue contributions. Additionally, the company's active class action lawsuit regarding algorithmic bias in its hiring tools poses a reputational and financial risk.

reasons.day: The recent underperformance relative to the sector suggests market skepticism about near-term AI revenue realization. However, the company's strong position in the Gartner Magic Quadrant and strategic AI partnerships provide a foundation for future growth.
reasons.medium: The acquisition of C1.ai addresses critical identity governance needs for AI agents, creating a strategic advantage in the agentic AI infrastructure space. This move, combined with partnerships with Straiker and OneTrust, strengthens Workday's position as a trust layer for enterprise AI.
reasons.long: Workday's three-tier AI framework and 'lawful AI' approach create a defensible moat in the agentic AI infrastructure space. The company's focus on human-in-the-loop AI and strategic partnerships with C1.ai, Straiker, and OneTrust position it as a critical trust layer for enterprise AI agents.
reasons.short: KeyBanc's downgrade to Sector Weight reflects concerns about delayed AI revenue contributions. While the company has strong AI capabilities, the lag in HR tech budget adoption could impact near-term financial performance.
